home.heroTitle2: how a coding agent finds its way
home.heroBody: Seven lessons with a live simulation: what a code graph is, which kinds exist, whether there is a standard, and what it all looks like in an organization of hundreds of repos and thousands of developers. No prior knowledge needed.
home.syllabusLead: What this course covers. A lesson you already finished is marked done.
home.curriculumNote: The course teaches general ideas. It describes no particular company, and the organization in the examples is made up.

built.search: Looks for letters in the files on the machine
built.syntax: Built by a parser, file by file. Knows names.
built.index: Built with the compiler. Knows each symbol exactly.
built.contract: Built from declared interfaces and their declared users.

callers.imprecise: Two definitions share this name and the graph matches by name. One of the two candidates is wrong.
callers.right: Only one definition with this name is left, so matching by name is enough.

callees.right: The calls are written in the function body, and a parser sees them.

fieldReaders.blind: One side has a string, the other a property. To the syntax they are unrelated.

callers.right: The compiler resolved each call to one definition.

callees.right: The same: each call is resolved to an exact symbol.

fieldReaders.blind: Each language has its own index, and an HTTP request between them is not a symbol.

index.unavailable: The compiler could not process the project, so there is usually no index for this commit.

fieldReaders.right: The field is part of a declared interface, and its reader is on record.

contract.blind: This happens inside the service. A contract knows only its boundary.

s.everyMachineOwn: Every machine indexes only its own

m.affected: Developers who lose it if one server fails
m.survives: Own work survives a central failure

topology.assumptions: Assumptions: developers are split evenly between servers, with no failover. In hybrid, "lose" means answers about other people's repos.
topology.figure: A diagram of an example organization in four lanes: product teams, platform, security and access, developers

edge.merge: A change is merged and triggers CI
edge.snapshot: CI stores a snapshot in the registry
edge.load: The server loads snapshots from the registry
edge.ask: The MCP client calls a tool on the server

does.ci: Runs after every merge, runs the indexer and stores the result.
does.registry: Records which snapshot belongs to which repo and which commit.
does.server: Takes questions from agents as tool calls and answers from the snapshots.
does.policy: The rule for who may read which repo. A snapshot inherits it from its repo.
does.machine: Runs the agent. Inside the agent there is one MCP client per server it is connected to.

repo.local: Only repos cloned to the machine are visible to the agent.
repo.other: Every merge triggers the publish of a new snapshot.

ci.used: One build per repo, not per machine.

registry.used: The one place the servers load from.

server.central: One server for all developers. Everyone depends on it.
server.hybrid: Answers about other people's repos. The local server answers about your working copy.
server.sharded: Each server serves part of the developers, and all serve the same snapshots.

policy.local: The only check is whether you could clone the repo.
policy.other: Has to be enforced at the registry, at the server, or both. See lesson 7.

machine.local: Builds its own graphs and runs a local server as a subprocess.
machine.central: Builds nothing. It only asks the central server.
machine.hybrid: Builds a graph of its own working copy and asks the central server about the rest.
machine.sharded: Asks the server it is assigned to.

step.q1: The agent needs a fact about code in another team's repo.
step.q2: The MCP client calls a tool on the server.
step.q3: The server checks what the caller may read.
step.q4: The server reads the snapshot listed in the registry.
step.q5: The answer returns to the agent, with the snapshot's commit.
step.h1: The agent needs two facts: one about your code and one about another team's.
step.h2: The local server answers about your working copy, uncommitted changes included.
step.h3: For the other repo the MCP client asks the central server.
step.h4: The central server checks access and reads the snapshot.
step.h5: The answer returns with its commit. The agent now has both facts.
step.l1: The agent needs a fact about code.
step.l2: The MCP client asks the local server, which runs on the same machine.
step.l3: The local server answers from a graph built from a cloned repo.
step.l4: For repos that were not cloned there is no one to ask.
step.p1: A change is merged into a repo.
step.p2: CI runs the indexer on the repo.
step.p3: The snapshot is stored and its commit is recorded in the registry.
step.p4: The servers load the new snapshot. Answers are current from now on.
step.n1: Nothing is published in this arrangement. Each machine indexes for itself.

access.share: Share of repos this developer may read
access.skipServer: The request skips the server and goes straight to the registry
access.serviceAccount: The server reads the registry with one account that may read everything
access.modelNote: A model of one common design, not a description of a product.
access.figure: The path of a request from the developer to the registry, with the places where access is checked

format.name: Data format
format.q: How is an index written to a file?
format.standard: Several formats are published openly, and each is well defined.
format.notStandard: No single format that everyone agreed on. Different tools read different formats.

indexer.name: Indexers
indexer.q: Who extracts the facts from the code?
indexer.standard: Nothing. These are open-source projects, one per language.
indexer.notStandard: Coverage differs by language, and not every language has a tool.

storage.name: Storage, query and registry
storage.q: Where are the facts kept, and how do you ask?
storage.standard: Nothing. There are open-source systems and accounts that companies have published.
storage.notStandard: The registry, meaning which snapshot belongs to which repo and commit, is built anew in each organization.

serving.name: Serving
serving.standard: How an agent discovers and calls tools.
serving.notStandard: Which tools a graph server offers and what they return. Whoever builds the server decides.

org.name: Organization metadata and contracts
org.q: Who owns what, and what are the interfaces?
org.standard: Formats for describing interfaces and for listing components.
org.notStandard: Joining code, contracts and ownership into one graph.

landscape.unknown: A company's internal setup is known only from what it has published. Everything else is unknown.

piece.lsif: A format from the LSP world, for navigating code without a local copy of the source.
piece.scip: An open protobuf schema for a code index. Designed by Sourcegraph, partly after pain points with LSIF.
piece.kythe-schema: The graph schema of Kythe, an open-source project from Google that aims at language-agnostic exchange of facts about code.
piece.tree-sitter: A parser generator and parsing library. Gives useful results even with syntax errors.
piece.scip-indexers: A separate tool per language, relying on that language's compiler or build setup.
piece.kythe-indexers: Tools that hook into the build and extract nodes and edges from it.
piece.codeql: Builds a database of the codebase for analysis. For compiled languages, by watching the build.
piece.glean: An open-source system from Meta for storing facts about code, with its own query language. Also takes in SCIP and LSIF.
piece.central-index: Google described in 2020 one central index for its code search: the work is done once, for everyone.
piece.registry: No standard and no agreed name. This course calls it a registry.
piece.mcp: An open specification: an agent discovers tools on a server and calls them. It is revised from time to time, so check the revision.
piece.lsp: The protocol between a code editor and a language server. LSIF grew out of it.
piece.graph-tools: The MCP specification does not cover this. Two servers can serve completely different graphs.
piece.backstage: An open-source software catalog: components, APIs and teams, with relations such as ownedBy and consumesApi. Its source of truth is descriptor files kept in source control.
piece.openapi: A language-agnostic description of an HTTP API.
piece.asyncapi: A description of message-driven and event-driven APIs.
piece.protobuf: A language-neutral, platform-neutral definition of structured data.
piece.graphql: A type system and query language. The schema describes what the service offers.
piece.spdx: An open standard for a software bill of materials (SBOM).
piece.cyclonedx: A bill-of-materials standard, published as ECMA-424.
piece.joining: No standard joins the three. "Contract graph" in this course names an idea, not a format.
